title: Scale Out
briefing: A popular newsletter just featured you. Traffic climbs from 1,000 to 5,000 requests per second.
Every request still needs 10ms of CPU time. The biggest app server available has 16 vCPUs.
A load balancer spreads requests evenly across every app server instance behind it.
debrief: No single machine can handle 5,000 req/s, so you scaled out: several machines behind a load balancer. This is horizontal scaling.
The back-of-envelope math: 5,000 req/s × 10ms = 50 vCPUs of work. Add headroom so nothing runs near 100% and you need about 64 vCPUs.

Round-robin load balancing sends every instance the same number of requests, whatever its size. Mix a small server in with big ones and the small one is overwhelmed while the big ones sit idle. Keep the instances in a pool identical, or use a weighted or least-connections algorithm.
Scaling out has another benefit you'll need in the next level: no single machine is a point of failure.

solutions.name: Four xlarge servers
solutions.explanation: 64 vCPUs give 6,400 req/s of capacity, about 78% busy at peak. Large instances have many vCPUs, so even at 78% a request rarely waits long.

solutions.name: Eight large servers
solutions.explanation: The same 64 vCPUs at the same price, spread over more machines. Smaller pieces are also cheaper to lose, which matters in the next level.

antiSolutions.name: One xlarge server
antiSolutions.explanation: The biggest machine available handles 1,600 req/s. Vertical scaling has hit its ceiling.

antiSolutions.name: Three xlarge servers
antiSolutions.explanation: 4,800 req/s of capacity looks close enough, but anything over 100% means the queue grows every second until requests time out.

antiSolutions.name: Three xlarge plus one medium
antiSolutions.explanation: 52 vCPUs in total, but round robin gives the medium server a quarter of the traffic: 1,250 req/s against its 400 req/s capacity.

antiSolutions.name: Five xlarge servers
antiSolutions.explanation: Works, but over budget. Headroom is good; paying for capacity you never use is not.

antiSolutions.name: Four instances with no load balancer
antiSolutions.explanation: Clients connect to one address. Without a load balancer there's nothing to spread their requests across the instances.
